title: Temporary shelter produces public health and safety benefits without clearly reducing future homelessness
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 34376, Los Angeles County homeless-services administrative records and shelter-availability variation
geography: Los Angeles County, California, United States

observations.period: 2014-2019 daily shelter-bed and service observations; winter-shelter availability shocks

denominator.unit: daily site-level homeless-service, shelter, crime, hospital, and mortality records; analytic counts are not disclosed in the abstract

shelter_route.unit: temporary shelter provision and variation in available beds from Los Angeles County winter-shelter programs

identification.unit: variation from shocks to shelter availability used to study the effects of providing temporary shelter

observations.method: The study constructs daily site-level counts of shelter beds and occupants, pairs them with block-level crime and hospital-level emergency-room data, and uses winter-shelter availability shocks to estimate effects of temporary shelter provision.
observations.uncertainty: The abstract does not disclose the full sample, effect sizes, or all assumptions behind the availability-shock design. Shelter access, service mix, neighborhood conditions, and public response may change together.
observations.subgroup: People experiencing unsheltered homelessness, shelter users, nearby residents, psychiatric emergency-room patients, and neighborhood-level crime/health outcomes are separate units.
observations.counterinterpretation: Shelter may reduce public harms while leaving future homelessness unchanged; observed area benefits do not prove durable housing, individual recovery, or equal access to shelter.

observations.period: Short-run and future outcomes following temporary shelter availability

denominator.unit: study-specific service, crime, hospital, and mortality observations

crime.unit: reducing unsheltered homelessness significantly reduces crime

psychiatric_er.unit: reducing unsheltered homelessness significantly reduces emergency-room visits for psychiatric conditions

future_homelessness.unit: no evidence temporary shelter reduces future homelessness more than street outreach or other non-shelter services

observations.method: Cross-domain outcome comparison using the administrative records and shelter-availability design described in the paper.
observations.uncertainty: Area-level crime and hospital effects are not the same as individual housing recovery. The null future-homelessness comparison may depend on service selection, follow-up horizon, shelter quality, and the alternative services available.
observations.subgroup: Public-safety, psychiatric-care, mortality, and future-homelessness outcomes are distinct endpoints and should not be collapsed into a single shelter-success score.
observations.counterinterpretation: A public good can generate benefits for neighbors and health systems even when the individual housing endpoint does not improve relative to other services.

related_sources.claim: Emergency financial assistance provides a separate housing-crisis-to-work route; shelter and cash assistance outcomes are not pooled.
HUD supportive-housing evaluation materials provide a distinct tenancy and service-use route.

boundary: This record supports a temporary-shelter-to-public-health-and-safety bridge with a future-homelessness null comparison. It does not establish durable housing, individual service adequacy, resident consent, trust, political action, or a universal shelter effect.
